anchor: Taste this, and be henceforth among the Gods
title: Eve's dream: 'Taste this, and be henceforth among the Gods'
short: The dream Satan whispered into Eve's ear rehearses the temptation of Book IX: flattery, the tasted fruit, and a flight above the earth.
body: Eve dreams that a voice like Adam's calls her out by night, that every eye in nature admires her beauty, and that one 'shap'd and wing'd like one of those from Heav'n' plucks and tastes the forbidden fruit, offering it with the promise 'Taste this, and be henceforth among the Gods Thy self a Goddess'. The promise echoes the serpent's 'ye shall be as gods' (Genesis 3:5), as Verity notes, and he calls the episode a foretaste of the full temptation in 9.494-833. Satan's 'in the Air' anticipates his title 'prince of the power of the air' (Ephesians 2:2). The Dartmouth edition observes how the dream prepares Eve to believe the serpent's later claim that he has eaten the fruit. The dream was produced by Satan 'Squat like a Toad' at her ear (4.799-809).

title: Fansie and Reason: Adam's theory of dreams
short: Adam explains Eve's dream by the faculty psychology of his day: when Reason sleeps, imitative Fancy combines images at random.
body: Adam consoles Eve with the standard Renaissance psychology of the soul's faculties: the senses supply images, 'Fansie next' (imagination) forms them into shapes, and Reason, chief of the faculties, judges and assents or refuses. In sleep Reason retires and 'mimic Fansie wakes To imitate her', producing 'wilde work' by joining things ill-matched, often fragments of 'our last Eevnings talk'. Verity notes that for Milton 'fancy' meant the highest imaginative power, 'internal sight' (8.461), and records Johnson's complaint that such philosophy sits oddly in a new-created man. Adam's key principle is that 'Evil into the mind of God or Man May come and go, so unapprov'd, and leave No spot or blame behind' (5.117-19): temptation is not sin unless the will consents, which matters for judging Eve's state before the Fall.

title: Adam and Eve's morning hymn: 'These are thy glorious works'
short: A spontaneous hymn of praise modelled on Psalm 148 and the Benedicite, calling on every part of creation to praise its maker.
body: Before work Adam and Eve pray in 'various style', not in set forms: Milton, who opposed fixed liturgies, makes their prayer spontaneous 'unmeditated' eloquence. Verity identifies the models: Psalm 148, in which sun, moon, stars, waters, beasts and kings are called upon to praise the Lord, and the canticle 'O all ye works of the Lord' (the Benedicite, sung at Morning Prayer in the Book of Common Prayer); the Dartmouth edition makes the same identification. The hymn names the morning star ('Fairest of Starrs'), the sun, moon, planets and elements, mists, winds and birds, ending with a prayer to be kept from evil 'if the night Have gathered aught of evil or conceald'. It shows the right relation of creature to creation that the Fall will disturb, and Thomson's Hymn (1730) imitates it.

title: Raphael, the sociable Spirit
short: The archangel sent to warn Adam: 'sociable' because in the Book of Tobit he travelled as a companion with Tobias and shared his meals.
body: Raphael's name means 'God has healed'. In the apocryphal Book of Tobit he travels in human disguise with young Tobias, guides him, and drives the demon Asmodeus from his bride Sara (Tobit 5-8), revealing at the end that he is 'one of the seven holy angels' (Tobit 12:15); Verity summarises the story in his note on 4.167-71, and the Dartmouth edition gives the etymology. Milton calls him 'the sociable Spirit, that deign'd To travel with Tobias', and the epithet defines his role: he comes as a friend, eats with Adam and Eve and talks with them for four books (V-VIII). God sends him so that Man may have no excuse: he is to warn Adam of his free will and his danger, 'Least wilfully transgressing he pretend Surprisal, unadmonisht, unforewarnd' (5.244-45).

title: A Phoenix, gaz'd by all ... six wings he wore
short: Descending to Eden, Raphael looks to the birds like the unique Phoenix flying to the Egyptian sun-temple; alighting, he is seen as a six-winged seraph.
body: To the birds Raphael appears 'A Phoenix, gaz'd by all, as that sole Bird When to enshrine his reliques in the Sun's Bright Temple, to Egyptian Theb's he flies'. Verity explains that only one Phoenix lived at a time (Ovid, Amores 2.6.54, 'unica semper avis'), and that it flew to the temple of the sun to bury its predecessor's remains; the Dartmouth edition notes that Milton, like his contemporaries, identified Heliopolis, the city of the sun, with Thebes. The bird's resurrection made it a Christian symbol of renewal. When he alights, Raphael takes 'his proper shape', a seraph with six wings (Isaiah 6:2), which Verity notes Milton varies with details from Ezekiel; two wings cover his breast 'with regal Ornament', two gird his waist with gold, and two cover his feet with sky-coloured feathers.

title: Like Maia's son he stood
short: Raphael is compared to Hermes, son of Maia, the gods' messenger, who in Homer and Virgil brings warnings to Odysseus and Aeneas.
body: Raphael stands 'Like Maia's son', Hermes (Mercury), son of Zeus and the nymph Maia, the winged messenger of the gods; Verity glosses the allusion. The comparison has pointed epic precedents, as the Dartmouth edition notes: Hermes descends to warn Odysseus against Circe and gives him the protective herb moly (Odyssey 10.275-306), and Mercury descends to Carthage to remind Aeneas of his duty and make him leave Dido (Aeneid 4.219-78). Raphael's mission is similar: a divine warning to a hero who is in danger through a woman's attraction, a theme Raphael himself raises in his rebuke to Adam at 8.561-94. Like Mercury, he is also a guide, and the classical image dignifies the domestic scene that follows.

anchor: Of three that in Mount Ida naked strove
title: fairest Goddess feign'd Of three that in Mount Ida naked strove
short: Eve is lovelier than Venus in the Judgment of Paris, the beauty contest whose prize of a golden apple led to the Trojan War.
body: Eve, 'Undeckt, save with her self', is more lovely than 'the fairest Goddess feign'd Of three that in Mount Ida naked strove'. Verity tells the story of the Judgment of Paris: Strife threw a golden apple inscribed 'to the fairest' among the guests at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis; Hera, Athena and Aphrodite claimed it, and the Trojan shepherd-prince Paris, judging on Mount Ida, gave it to Aphrodite, who rewarded him with Helen, causing the Trojan War. The Dartmouth edition cites Ovid's Heroides 5. The comparison is dangerous praise: it links Eve's beauty with a fatal apple, a judgment of the senses, and the origin of the greatest war of classical epic, and the word 'feign'd' again marks the myth as fiction.

title: Haile Mother of Mankind
short: Raphael greets Eve with the angel's 'Hail' of the Annunciation to Mary, marking her as a type of the 'second Eve' who will bear the Redeemer.
body: Raphael's salutation, 'Haile Mother of Mankind, whose fruitful Womb Shall fill the World more numerous with thy Sons Then with these various fruits the Trees of God Have heap'd this Table', deliberately echoes Gabriel's greeting to Mary, 'Hail, thou that art highly favoured' (Luke 1:28); the narrator repeats the 'holy salutation us'd Long after to blest Marie, second Eve' (5.386-87). Verity cites Luke and compares Paul's calling Christ 'the last Adam' (1 Corinthians 15:45). The typology of Mary as the second Eve, whose obedience undoes the first Eve's disobedience, goes back to the early Church Fathers. The Dartmouth edition observes that the blessing envisages only sons. The fertile womb set beside the heaped fruit makes the coming temptation by fruit the more poignant.

title: To transubstantiate ... the Empiric Alchimist
short: Raphael really eats and digests earthly food, turning it into angelic substance: a deliberate jab at Catholic doctrine and at theologians who said angels only seemed to eat.
body: Raphael eats 'not seemingly ... nor in mist, the common gloss Of Theologians, but with keen dispatch Of real hunger, and concoctive heate To transubstantiate'. Verity quotes Newton: several Fathers held that angels only appeared to eat, citing Tobit 12:19, where Raphael says 'I did neither eat nor drink, but you did see a vision'. Milton rejects this. His word for digestion, 'transubstantiate', is the term of the Catholic doctrine of the Eucharist, which he rejected, and the Dartmouth edition notes the pointed reapplication: real change of substance happens in angelic digestion, not at the altar. The comparison with the 'Empiric Alchimist' turning 'drossiest Ore' to gold (Verity glosses empiric as 'experimenting', with a hint of 'quack') continues the alchemical imagery of Book III. The passage illustrates Milton's monist view that spirit and matter differ in degree, not kind.

title: one first matter all: the scale of nature
short: Raphael's statement of Milton's monism: all things come from God, made of one matter refined by degrees from body up to spirit, like a plant from root to flower.
body: Raphael explains: 'one Almightie is, from whom All things proceed, and up to him return, If not deprav'd from good, created all Such to perfection, one first matter all'. Things are 'more refin'd, more spiritous, and pure' the nearer they are to God, as a plant rises from root to stalk to leaves to the 'bright consummate floure', whose fruit nourishes the 'vital spirits' and finally intellect (5.479-87). Verity quotes Christian Doctrine 1.7, where Milton describes the original matter as good, derived from God himself, and notes the related idea in Comus that body may 'by degrees' turn to soul. The Dartmouth edition calls this the most explicit statement of Milton's monism. Raphael adds that human bodies 'may at last turn all to Spirit' and ascend, 'If ye be found obedient' (5.497-501).

title: Discursive, or Intuitive
greek: Latin discursus, 'running to and fro'; intueri, 'to look into'
short: Two modes of reason: human reason is mostly discursive, reasoning step by step; angelic reason mostly intuitive, seeing truth at once. They differ 'in degree, of kind the same'.
body: The soul's being is reason, which is 'Discursive, or Intuitive; discourse Is oftest yours, the latter most is ours, Differing but in degree, of kind the same'. Verity explains the old distinction: intuition (Latin intueri, 'to look into') grasps truth immediately, while 'discourse', in its older sense, reaches it through a chain of reasoning; Milton, in Christian Doctrine 1.9, likewise gives the good angels a higher, more immediate knowledge. The scholastic tradition, as in Aquinas, made the difference one of kind; Milton's insistence that it is only of degree fits his monism and his hope that humans may rise toward angelic being. It also gives weight to the long conversation between angel and man in Books V-VIII as an exchange between kindred minds.

title: freely we serve, Because wee freely love
short: Raphael tells Adam that angelic obedience is free: they serve because they love, and some, by not loving, have fallen.
body: Adam asks how he and Eve could ever fail in obedience to such a Maker. Raphael answers that God made Adam 'perfet, not immutable', and left his good 'in thy power': 'God made thee perfet, not immutable; And good he made thee, but to persevere He left it in thy power, ordaind thy will By nature free'. The angels likewise: 'freely we serve, Because wee freely love, as in our will To love or not; in this we stand or fall'. Verity cites Christian Doctrine 1.3, where God lets men and angels stand or fall at their own choice. The passage restates the Father's argument of Book III in friendlier terms, and its last words introduce Raphael's story of how 'som are fall'n'. The Dartmouth edition points to Milton's longer treatment of free will in Christian Doctrine 1.4.

anchor: By lik'ning spiritual to corporal forms
title: By lik'ning spiritual to corporal forms ... the shaddow of Heav'n
short: Raphael will describe the war in Heaven in bodily terms Adam can grasp, adding that earth may be more like Heaven than men think.
body: Raphael faces the problem of telling 'invisible exploits Of warring Spirits' to a human listener. He will proceed 'By lik'ning spiritual to corporal forms, As may express them best', the method theologians called accommodation, by which Scripture speaks of God in human terms. But he adds a startling qualification: 'though what if Earth Be but the shaddow of Heav'n, and things therein Each to other like, more then on earth is thought?' The Dartmouth edition compares Plato's cave (Republic 514a) but notes that Milton stresses likeness rather than difference, in keeping with his monism. The passage is central to debates about how literally to read the war in Heaven, with its cannon and armour: is it allegory, accommodation, or a description of real spiritual bodies?

title: Thrones, Dominations, Princedoms, Vertues, Powers
greek: Greek thronoi, kuriotêtes, archai, dunameis, exousiai
short: The formal roll-call of angelic orders, from Paul's list in Colossians and the ninefold hierarchy of Pseudo-Dionysius; it recurs, with irony, in Satan's speeches.
body: God addresses the angels by five of their traditional ranks. Paul lists 'thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers' (Colossians 1:16; compare Ephesians 1:21), and the fifth-century writer known as Dionysius the Areopagite arranged nine orders in three triads (Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones; Dominations, Virtues, Powers; Principalities, Archangels, Angels), a scheme the Dartmouth edition cites. Milton uses the titles loosely and never commits to the full system. The line recurs as a formula: Satan uses it to open his seditious speech, adding sarcastically 'If these magnific Titles yet remain Not merely titular' (5.772-74), and Abdiel throws it back at him (5.840). The repetition turns a liturgical roll-call into a political argument about rank and liberty.

title: This day I have begot whom I declare My onely Son
short: The chronologically first event of the poem: the Father proclaims the Son head of the angels, quoting Psalm 2:7. What 'begot' means here is a famous crux.
body: The Father declares to the assembled angels: 'This day I have begot whom I declare My onely Son, and on this holy Hill Him have anointed, whom ye now behold At my right hand' (5.603-06). The words are from Psalm 2:6-7, 'Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee', applied to Christ in Hebrews 1:5; 'anointed' translates 'Messiah', as Verity notes. Verity reads the passage as evidence of Milton's Arianism. Critics have long debated the sense of 'begot': since the Son was already active (he created the angels, 5.835-37), most take it as a metaphorical begetting, an exaltation to kingship, as Milton argues in Christian Doctrine 1.5; others see the Son's creation itself. The Dartmouth edition notes that obedience to the Son functions in Heaven as the forbidden tree does on earth. Satan's envy of this exaltation starts the rebellion.

title: mystical dance ... mazes intricate, Eccentric, intervolv'd
short: The angels' festal dance imitates the planets' apparently irregular motions, which are 'regular Then most, when most irregular they seem'.
body: The angels celebrate with 'Mystical dance, which yonder starrie Spheare Of Planets and of fixt in all her Wheeles Resembles nearest, mazes intricate, Eccentric, intervolv'd, yet regular Then most, when most irregular they seem'. Verity connects the image with the music of the spheres and explains 'eccentric' in its astronomical sense of orbits not centred on the earth; the Dartmouth edition notes that eccentrics were devices of Ptolemaic astronomy for explaining apparent anomalies. The idea that celestial order is hidden in apparent irregularity is ancient (Plato's Timaeus) and fits the poem's theodicy: what seems disorderly in providence may be most ordered. Contrast the devils, who reason 'in wandring mazes lost' (2.561).

title: The Palace of great Lucifer ... The Mountain of the Congregation
short: Satan withdraws his legions to the North, to a palace on a mount he calls the Mountain of the Congregation, enacting Isaiah's prophecy of Lucifer's pride.
body: Raphael names Satan's former seat 'The Palace of great Lucifer (so call That Structure in the Dialect of men Interpreted)'. Lucifer, 'light-bringer', is the Latin name of the morning star, used in the Vulgate of Isaiah 14:12, 'How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!' The next verse supplies the rest: 'I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north'. Verity explains that demonological tradition therefore placed Lucifer in the north, and the Dartmouth edition notes the same source for 'the Quarters of the North' (5.689). Satan's countenance, 'as the Morning Starr that guides The starrie flock', draws a third of the angels after him (Revelation 12:4). Milton's parenthesis keeps the name a human translation.

title: self-begot, self-rais'd By our own quick'ning power
short: Satan denies that God or the Son created the angels: they arose of themselves by fate. The claim contradicts his own admission in Book IV.
body: Answering Abdiel's reminder that the Son made all the angels, Satan asks who saw their creation: 'We know no time when we were not as now; Know none before us, self-begot, self-rais'd By our own quick'ning power, when fatal course Had circl'd his full Orbe'. Verity compares Adam's account of his own awakening in Book VIII (8.250-82): ignorant like Satan of his origin, Adam at once infers a maker, 'how came I thus, how here?', while Satan refuses one. Newton (quoted by Verity) remarked that Milton makes Satan a fatalist, 'No compliment to fatalism'. The Dartmouth edition compares Satan's private admission on Niphates that God 'created what I was' (4.43). Self-creation is the logical root of the rebellion: a being who owes nothing can owe no obedience.

title: Abdiel, faithful found Among the faithless
short: The one seraph who stands up to Satan and walks out alone; his name means 'servant of God', and many readers see Milton's own isolation after 1660 in him.
body: Abdiel's name, as Verity and the Dartmouth edition note, means 'servant of God'; it occurs in Scripture only as a man's name (1 Chronicles 5:15). Milton makes him the seraph who alone answers Satan's sedition, arguing that God, who made the angels through the Son, cannot be unjust to them. When he leaves, 'Among the faithless, faithful only hee; Among innumerable false, unmov'd, Unshak'n, unseduc'd, unterrifi'd' (5.897-99). Verity notes the pattern of negative epithets and suggests that Milton may have thought of his own position at the Restoration, when he stood almost alone for the defeated republic. Abdiel's departure echoes Moses' warning to depart from the tents of the rebel Korah (Numbers 16:26), which Verity and the Dartmouth edition cite. He is welcomed in Book VI: 'Servant of God, well done' (6.29).
